item.title: Ontario premier wants Republicans to lose House and Senate over Trump's trade war
item.description: Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he hopes Republicans lose the House and Senate in the midterms to hold President Donald Trump accountable for the trade war with Canada.
item.content:encoded:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Thursday that he hopes Republicans in the U.S. lose both the House and Senate in the upcoming midterm elections, suggesting that voters should punish President Donald Trump for his moves to escalate the ongoing trade war with Canada.

"Hopefully, he's going to lose the Senate. He's going to lose Congress. I hope so, and hold him accountable," Ford said.

"But we'll see how that goes. We aren’t going to interfere in the U.S. election," he continued.

Ford has become one of Trump’s most outspoken critics in Canada, accusing the president of attempting to move Ontario’s businesses and jobs across the border to the U.S.

CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT

"He’s not reliable at all," Ford said. "He could make a deal today and then change his mind. And we’ve seen that over and over again."

Ford said he still believes Trump would like to reach a deal before the midterms and that Canada should return to the negotiation table as soon as possible.

"I truly believe President Trump wants a deal before the midterms," Ford said. "I could be wrong, but I think it’s best that we sit down and get a deal."

Ford’s comments come just days after the U.S. escalated the trade dispute by banning some Canadian dairy products and motorcycles as well most alcoholic beverages after Canada's retaliatory tariffs took effect on about $20 billion in U.S. goods.

Trump also took efforts to remove Canadian products from large, long-term U.S. government contracts.

Last year, Trump abruptly ended trade talks with Canada after the Ontario government broadcast an anti-tariff TV ad in the U.S., using quotes from former Republican President Ronald Reagan's criticism of tariffs.

Trump and Ford have repeatedly exchanged personal jabs over the trade war.

NEW YORK GOV HOCHUL REJECTS TRUMP'S 'LAKE AMERICA' RENAMING WITH BLUNT MESSAGE

Ford mocked Trump for keeping a portrait of Reagan near his desk while pushing for tariffs the former president had opposed, telling The Associated Press that Reagan would be "throwing up on him from the picture if he knew what was going on."

Trump, meanwhile, has criticized Ford as "the less charismatic, intelligent, and overall unimpressive brother of the late, great, Rob Ford."

The U.S. president further escalated tensions with Canada when he signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America," a rebranding that Canada does not recognize.

Canada, other international bodies and U.S. states are not forced to follow the renaming, but the order adds to the ongoing tensions between the two countries.

Ford said on Thursday that Trump had unintentionally strengthened Canada by forcing it to cut its dependence on the U.S.

"The only two good things Donald Trump has ever done for Canada" were that "he woke us up" and "he united the country like I’ve never seen before," Ford said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested on Thursday that his country may hold off on further retaliation against Trump’s latest trade measures, describing them as "relatively modest" compared to earlier U.S. moves.

He said his government was still studying the U.S. measures and acknowledged they could have significant consequences for companies and industries, but he said that some of the new U.S. tariffs replaced others that the Trump administration had removed.

"We also recognize that, in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done ... that these are relatively modest measures," Carney said at a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alberta.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Mamdani heads to 9/11 memorial despite 110,000-signature push from victims’ families to stay away
item.description: Scores of New Yorkers and 9/11 families signed a petition urging Zohran Mamdani to skip the Ground Zero memorial over his Ramzi Kassem pick.
item.content:encoded:
Scores of New Yorkers, including some families victimized by the Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the World Trade Center, are asking New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to skip the annual memorial service at Ground Zero — a call he is not heeding.

Mamdani is set to attend the annual remembrance ceremony on Friday at Ground Zero, which is an invitation-only event attended by victims’ families, dignitaries and other invited guests. Hosted by the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, the event begins at 8:30 a.m. Vice President JD Vance and former presidents Joe Biden, Barack Obama, Bill Clinton and George W. Bush are also expected to attend.

A petition launched by relatives of 9/11 victims, which has since garnered roughly 110,000 signatures, asks Mamdani to stay home on Friday, citing his appointment of Ramzi Kassem as the city's chief legal counsel. Kassem previously represented Ahmed al-Darbi, an al Qaeda operative who pleaded guilty to war-crimes charges.

"For 9/11 families, this is not simply a public ceremony—it is a deeply personal day of mourning. The presence of individuals whose words or associations are perceived as conflicting with the solemn purpose of the event risks detracting from that focus and causing additional pain," the petition reads.

9/11 FAMILIES PUSH TO BAN MAMDANI FROM 25TH ANNIVERSARY REMEMBRANCE OVER 'HOSTILE' RECORD

"The 25th anniversary should remain centered on remembrance, unity, and an unambiguous rejection of the violence and extremism that defined that day. Ensuring that all participants reflect these principles is essential to preserving the integrity of the commemoration."

The controversy intensified after Mamdani handed a ceremonial pen used to sign 9/11-related executive orders to NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and asked her to pass it to Kassem. Critics on social media characterized the hand-off as a slap in the face to relatives of those who died in the attacks.

The mayor has defended his decision to attend the 9/11 memorial despite the criticisms levied against him.

"I'm proud to be the mayor of this city. I love this city. I love this country. And what I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers," Mamdani said in response to the criticisms.

MAMDANI UNDER FIRE AFTER SYMBOLIC 9/11 PEN GOES TO FORMER AL QAEDA DEFENSE LAWYER

Former New York Gov. George Pataki and one-time New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, both Republicans, have echoed calls for Mamdani to stay away from the ceremony.

"Having lost friends there and being very close to many of the families, it offends me that he’s coming," the former mayor said.

​In addition to his appointment of Kassem, Mamdani has also caught flak from critics in the lead-up to Sept. 11 for his past failure to denounce the phrase "globalize the intifada," his praise for an unindicted co-conspirator in the 1993 World Trade Center bombing, his endorsement of candidates who have made controversial statements about the attack and his continued association with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who stated that America "deserved 9/11."

HASAN PIKER STANDS BY 'INTENTIONALLY PROVOCATIVE' CLAIMS THAT HAMAS IS 'A THOUSAND TIMES BETTER' THAN ISRAEL

The mayor later called Piker’s comments "objectionable and reprehensible," though has not disavowed him as a figure. He has also since stated that he would "discourage" people from saying "globalize the intifada."

The mayor’s office did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

item.title: 9/11 hero’s legacy lives on 25 years later as son unveils new tech lifeline for those facing grief
item.description: Doora, an AI grief chatbot from nonprofit Hold the Door, launched on the 9/11 anniversary to honor a father killed in the World Trade Center.
item.content:encoded:
A father's legacy is living on through a new artificial intelligence (AI) tool that helps others navigate grief and trauma — two-and-a-half decades after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Launched on the 25th anniversary of the horrific attacks on U.S. soil, Doora is a new AI grief companion from Hold the Door, a nonprofit founded in memory of Ronald Fazio Sr., who was killed after helping his coworkers evacuate the South Tower of the World Trade Center.

"We designed Doora to be a bridge for people in the moment when they're going through a very difficult time so they can have a moment... where they say, 'Maybe I can get through this. Maybe I can grow from this experience,'" Rob Fazio, Fazio Sr.'s son and founder of Hold the Door, told Fox News Digital.

"The foundation of Doora is built upon our 24 years of experience and research on post-traumatic growth and growth through loss and adversity."

HAWLEY CHAMPIONS GUARD ACT AS HEARTBROKEN FAMILIES SAY AI CHATBOTS ALLEGEDLY PUSHED TEENS TO SELF-HARM

The 24/7 chatbot, which Fazio described as a "growth guide," offers voice and text support to help people navigate grief when therapy or support from counselors, friends or family isn't an option.

In a world increasingly skeptical but reliant on AI tools, a team of lawyers, psychologists and business leaders worked together to create Doora specifically for people who are hesitant to seek help.

"Where we used to have people come to us, we realized that going to people and meeting them where they are physically, emotionally and psychologically gets much better results," he said.

Every Hold the Door initiative, including the new AI tool launch, is intended to honor his father and his final act of heroism, according to Fazio.

"His natural instinct of putting others first was really the birth of Hold the Door for others," he recalled of his father. "That's what me and my family have done for the last 25 years."

Hold the Door also offers free workshops, grief resources and community programs inspired by the resilience that followed 9/11.

9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY

Fazio said grieving without his father's remains brought unique challenges that he and his family had to work through. At the memorial service, they filled a coffin with treasured belongings that reflected the life his father lived.

"In the absence of a body, sometimes it is hard to grieve," he said.

That day, Fazio made a promise that would later inspire his nonprofit.

"I'll never forget, I was in a Catholic church when we were doing the service, and I said, 'You know, my dad was a quiet man, but his legacy is going to be damn loud,'" he said.

That promise now lives on through Hold the Door and Doora, which Fazio said is designed to "really walk with users" through grief.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

"We really are supportive and at the same time give people a little nudge toward their future while they're honoring a loved one they lost or some adversity that they faced," he said.

When grief feels overwhelming, Fazio said Doora can help people keep their pain from defining who they are or what comes next.

"You are who you are, and we can help you develop and create more of who you want to be," he said.

item.title: Republican cavalry arrives for Ken Paxton as big-bucks Texas offensive opens cash floodgates
item.description: Top Senate Republicans are pouring eight figures into a new Texas PAC to boost Ken Paxton against James Talarico in a razor-thin Senate showdown.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Top Senate Republicans are unleashing millions of dollars into Texas to ensure that the GOP holds on to the seat as the midterm elections close in.

The Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC tied to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., plans to launch the Texas PAC, unlocking a war chest of campaign funds to ensure Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton wins out in November.

Paxton is in a tight race against Texas State Rep. James Talarico, who has become a prime target for Republicans who argue that the state lawmaker is too progressive for deep red Texas.

THUNE-ALIGNED GROUPS UNLEASH HISTORIC WAR CHEST TO DEFEND SENATE MAJORITY: 'WINNING MESSAGE'

"As the Democrat Party gets pulled further to the left, extreme candidates like James Talarico are becoming the norm," Thune told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Republicans are united in keeping him out of the U.S. Senate, which is why I’m proud of the work the Senate Leadership Fund is doing to ensure Texas stays red."

A source familiar told Fox News Digital that during the convention’s final day on Thursday, Thune attended a fundraiser for Paxton to help boost his campaign.

The new PAC will launch an initial eight-figure ad buy on Friday, the day after the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas is set to wrap up. The group tells Fox News Digital they plan to run ads continuously through Election Day in Texas, and the first two will paint Paxton in a positive light, with another showing the contrast between the candidates.

LONGTIME GOP AIDE DEFECTS TO DEM RISING STAR AS TEXAS SENATE BATTLE FOR CORNYN'S SEAT HEATS UP

While the convention has been used to energize President Donald Trump’s base to get out and vote in tight contests across the country, the Texas Senate race was of particular emphasis. And the flow of cash to support cash marks a pivot for the Senate Republican leadership, who earlier in the year, threw their full support behind Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas.

But Trump’s endorsement of Paxton over Cornyn ultimately ended the longtime lawmaker’s bid, and set up a messy period of making amends after the dust settled in their runoff race.

Now, Republicans are showing a unified front and working to help Paxton financially as he tries to stave off Talarico.

Most of the latest public opinion surveys in the Senate showdown indicate Talarico with a slight single-digit edge over Paxton. The most recent Fox News poll, which was conducted at the end of July, indicated Talarico with a 51%-48% margin over Paxton.

The race is one of roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP holds its Senate majority in the midterms.

The launch of the Texas PAC comes a week after MAGA, Inc., the super PAC linked to President Donald Trump, made its first major midterm buy with $10 million in ad spending to support Paxton.

REPUBLICAN SOUNDS ALARM ON RISING DEM STAR: 'THIS GUY’S GOING TO BE A PROBLEM'

The support from the Texas PAC and MAGA Inc. is a boost for Paxton, with Talarico’s campaign holding a massive campaign cash advantage over Paxton’s campaign heading into the final stretch leading up to November’s midterms. Talarico has hauled in over $72 million in fundraising since launching his Senate campaign last year, compared to roughly $17 million by Paxton, according to federal filings.

Paxton told Fox News’ Bret Baier he had a "three-month fundraising difference" compared to Talarico thanks to the messy primary battle that dragged into May, months after the insurgent progressive toppled Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas.

"Talarico had three extra months to raise money and not spend it. So he was able to start spending on ads that tried to pivot him from a radical socialist to a moderate Democrat," Paxton said.

"So he's been running ads for about two months," he continued. "My ads have just started. We had to raise some money. But once we're able to highlight the stark differences between a socialist and a constitutional Republican, he will not win Texas."

item.title: JOHN ONDRASIK: What 9/11 taught us about courage, unity and the price of freedom
item.description: The song "Tuesday" honors September 11 victims as its creator asks whether America could still unite if another 9/11-scale attack struck today.
item.content:encoded:
9/11 occurred on a Tuesday.

In October 2009, I released a song entitled "Tuesday" — a musical plea to never forget the lessons of September 11, 2001, when Islamic terrorists murdered 2,977 innocent people on American soil.

Is Monday coming back

That’s what Mondays do

They turn and turn around

Afraid to see it through

Welcome to Monday.

9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS

Performing my song "Superman" at Paul McCartney’s Concert for New York City was one of the great honors of my life. To spend that day — and share that stage — with heroic New York City first responders and the families of those murdered was an incredibly humbling, life-changing experience.

Much of the audience at Madison Square Garden consisted of firefighters, police officers, rescue workers and others who had spent the previous month sifting through the rubble and carnage of Ground Zero. The images of thousands of people singing, screaming, crying and embracing one another remain seared into my memory. For a few hours, music gave them — and all of us — a chance to release some of the pain we carried within.

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

The world sang and cried with us.

You may remember what happened in the aftermath of 9/11. America came together in a way we had rarely seen before and have not seen since. There was no red America and blue America. There was only red, white and blue.

Americans stood shoulder to shoulder across the country with compassion, love and resolve — and with an unequivocal commitment to bring Osama bin Laden and his terrorist network to justice.

The thing about memories

They’re sure and bound to fade

Except for the stolen souls

Left upon her blade

Imagine standing in your neighborhood on September 12, 2001, and telling your neighbor what America might look like 25 years later.

Imagine telling them that radical leftist ideologies, hostile to America , would infiltrate some of our most prestigious universities and metastasize through mainstream and social media. That members of Congress would echo propaganda promoted by terrorist

DAVID MARCUS: CALLING 9/11 'INEVITABLE' IS SAME AS JUSTIFYING IT, AND IT IS DISGRACEFUL

organizations such as Hamas. That candidates could associate with people who openly express hatred for America—or even suggest America deserved 9/11—and still win elections and govern American cities.

They would not have believe you, such lunacy!

The aftermath of Hamas’s October 7 terrorist attack in Israel provided another warning about the moral collapse taking hold within many of our institutions. Before Israel had even buried its dead, we witnessed people in the West rationalizing, excusing and even celebrating the slaughter.

It raises an uncomfortable question: If an attack on the scale of 9/11 occurred in America today, would we still respond as one people, one country?

Or would we see more mob like campus encampments, ideological justifications for terrorism, and Americans blaming their own country as the "oppressor" that somehow got what it deserved.

Tuesday came and went

One September

When will she come again?

Twenty-five years after 9/11, America finds itself in another battle — this one for the soul of our nation and, more broadly, for the future of Western civilization.

The threats are not identical to those we faced in 2001. But they are real. Radical Islamism remains a global threat, while antisemitism and anti-American extremism increasingly find expression across the ideological spectrum. Ideas once confined to society’s fringes now travel instantly, and with little consequence, through universities, political movements and social media. The enemy is in the building, and time is not on our side.

That is why "Never Forget" cannot become merely a slogan printed on a bumper sticker or repeated once every September.

It is an obligation. It is our obligation.

We have a duty to teach our children what happened on September 11, 2001: about the evil fanatics who attacked us, why they attacked us, and the carnage of what unchecked extremism can produce.

But "Never Forget" means something more.

It means remembering the best of us.

It means telling our children about the firefighters who climbed stairwells while everyone else was running down. The police officers, paramedics and ordinary citizens who ran toward collapsing infernos to save people they had never met. The passengers of Flight 93 who understood what was happening and, knowing the probable cost, fought back.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

They represent the best of humanity.

Twenty-five years later, their courage should still challenge and inspire us.

Their sacrifice should remind us that America is not sustained merely by institutions, elections or slogans. It survives because generation after generation chooses to defend the principles that make the country worth defending.

Memory fades. History becomes distant. Tuesdays come and go.

But some Tuesdays must never be forgotten.

May the memory of those we lost — and the example of the heroes of September 11, 2001 — give us the strength, courage and fortitude to fight for America every day, especially Tuesdays, for the next 250 years.

Let’s Roll…

item.title: The Hispanic vote is up for grabs in 2026. Candidates who ignore it will lose
item.description: Hispanic voters in battleground districts remain persuadable heading into 2026, with over half undecided and cost of living topping their concerns.
item.content:encoded:
Hispanic voters are sending both parties a message that should be impossible to ignore: stop assuming you already know where we stand.

A record 36.2 million Hispanic Americans were eligible to vote in 2024. Heading into 2026, polling in competitive congressional districts suggests many are still persuadable, with more than half either undecided or open to changing their vote.

For years, political analysts have tried to squeeze Hispanic voters into a simple narrative. After one election, we're told Latinos are firmly in the Democratic camp. After the next, we're told Republicans have permanently reshaped the electorate.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS DEMOCRATS TURN LEFT, BLACK VOTERS TAP THE BRAKES

The reality is much less tidy.

Hispanic Americans are not moving in lockstep in either direction. They weigh candidates, priorities and circumstances, then make their own decisions. That’s what makes this electorate so consequential, and so risky for either party to take for granted.

When we ask Hispanic voters what matters most, the issues may sound familiar: the cost of living, housing, good jobs, health care and opportunity. But how those pressures are experienced matters.

Nine in ten Hispanic voters we surveyed in battleground districts cite the cost of living as a top issue, while 73% say they are surviving rather than getting ahead. Eight in ten are helping support family members outside their own household. These voters don't need generic messages about the economy. They want candidates who understand how economic pressures are affecting their families and communities, and who can speak credibly to their aspirations for getting ahead.

What often gets missed in political conversations is that Hispanic voters are more than a demographic category. They are parents, workers, business owners, neighbors, and community members. They want elected officials who understand those realities, not campaigns built around assumptions.

The encouraging news is that engagement remains strong.

MARINE COMBAT VETERAN BETS BIG ON HISPANIC OUTREACH IN BID TO FLIP DEM-HELD HOUSE SEAT

A recent Univision survey of registered Hispanic voters in Texas found overwhelming interest in participating this fall. Yet 69% said candidates pay too little attention to the interests and concerns of the Hispanic community.

That's a striking combination. These are not voters who have tuned out politics. If anything, many are paying close attention and wondering whether anyone is listening in return.

NEW MIDTERM BATTLEGROUND TAKES SHAPE AS PARTIES BUILD ELECTION ARMIES

Communication matters.

Seventy-one percent say it's important for candidates to communicate with voters in Spanish, while 56% say doing so would make them view a candidate more favorably.

TO WIN IN NOVEMBER, REPUBLICANS NEED TO TAKE A PAGE FROM OBAMA’S PLAYBOOK

That finding deserves more attention from campaigns. Speaking to Hispanic voters in Spanish isn't simply about translating an English-language message. It signals something more fundamental: that a candidate sees this electorate, respects it and is willing to make the effort to engage it directly.

In recent elections, candidates who have made the effort to engage Hispanic voters directly have had an advantage with this electorate. In close races this fall, Hispanic voters will help determine who wins and who loses; and Spanish-language engagement is an important part of earning their support.

When a candidate communicates in the language people use with family members and longtime friends, it sends a signal that the relationship matters. It suggests a willingness to meet voters where they are rather than expecting them to come to you.

But language alone isn't enough.

Campaigns have more tools than ever to identify and reach Hispanic voters. The harder task is connecting with them. That requires understanding how the issues shaping this election are experienced within Hispanic communities and communicating in ways that are relevant to their lives.

A campaign can flood someone's screen with messages. Earning someone's vote is harder. It takes consistency, respect and a demonstrated understanding of the community a candidate hopes to represent.

That's why Hispanic voters will help determine the outcome of some of the most competitive races in 2026. The electorate is large, engaged, growing and competitive.

Most importantly, Hispanic voters are making their own choices. They are not waiting for party strategists, pundits or political consultants to define them.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

The candidates who succeed will recognize that reality early. They'll talk seriously about affordability, economic opportunity, and the challenges families face every day. They'll show up consistently, not just in the final weeks before Election Day. And they'll approach Hispanic communities as voters to be persuaded, not constituencies to be claimed.

No party has a permanent hold on this electorate.

In 2026, the candidates who understand that first will be better positioned to win.

item.title: Trump set to honor 9/11 victims, first responders at Pentagon on 25th anniversary
item.description: President Donald Trump will attend a Pentagon ceremony on the 25th anniversary of 9/11 while JD Vance joins former presidents at the World Trade Center.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump will commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks at the Pentagon on Friday, honoring the victims and first responders who lost their lives that day.

"As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001," White House principal deputy press secretary Anna Kelly told Fox News Digital.

"On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans," Kelly added.

TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

Trump will attend a 9/11 remembrance ceremony at the Pentagon, while Vice President JD Vance will commemorate the attacks at the World Trade Center site in New York. Other administration officials will gather in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, ensuring the White House has a presence at all three sites tied to the Sept. 11 attacks.

Vance will join former presidents Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton, as well as former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani in New York for a remembrance ceremony.

Last year, Trump and first lady Melania Trump attended a 9/11 commemoration at the Pentagon and issued a Patriot Day proclamation calling for flags to be flown at half-staff.

He later attended a Yankees-Tigers game featuring tributes to the victims in the Bronx, New York City.

FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP’S 9/11 TRIBUTE TO FEATURE MASSIVE PIECE OF GROUND ZERO HISTORY AT WHITE HOUSE'

During his first term, Trump attended the Pentagon for a memorial in 2017 and 2019, then spent 9/11 at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania in 2018 and 2020.

Trump was a real-estate developer in New York City at the time of the attacks and watched the tragedy unfold in real time. 

"I have a window that looks directly at the World Trade Center, and I saw this huge explosion. I was with a group of people and I really couldn’t even believe it," Trump said in a phone interview with WWOR-TV channel 9 on the tragic day.

9/11 TAUGHT US DEADLY LESSONS. 25 YEARS LATER, WE NEED A NEW MODEL TO PREVENT ATTACKS

WHERE TUNNEL TO TOWERS' STEEL ACROSS AMERICA TOUR WILL STOP AHEAD OF 9/11

On Tuesday, the Tunnel to Towers Foundation brought its "Steel Across America" tour to Trump's doorstep at the White House, where the 21-foot, 16,900-pound steel beam recovered from the World Trade Center’s South Tower was on display.

The steel beam has served as a traveling memorial to the victims and first responders of 9/11, offering pop-up events across 21 states leading up to the anniversary of the tragic day.

item.title: Trump issues blunt midterm warning, Vance greeted with ‘48’ chants: Top takeaways from GOP convention
item.description: President Donald Trump led the Dallas crowd in a voting pledge and warned supporters they'd "go to hell" if they skip the midterm elections this November.
item.content:encoded:
Facing a brutal political environment as the GOP fights to hold control of Congress, President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance used their speeches on the concluding night of the first ever Republican midterm convention to paint clear contrasts with Democrats and energize supporters to vote.

With less than two months until the midterm elections — and early voting kicking off in a couple of weeks — Trump showcased his policy wins since returning to the White House and led the crowd at American Airlines Center in Dallas in an oath to vote as he made his second primetime convention appearance in two nights.

"You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell," the president warned.

Vance, in a strikingly partisan keynote address, charged that the Democratic Party is the "party of hatred." And with the next race for the White House kicking off once the midterms are over, Vance, the likely heir apparent for the term-limited Trump, was showered with chants of "48" – as in the 48th president – as he delivered his address.

VANCE SHUTS DOWN HECKLER WAVING MEXICAN FLAG

The speeches by Vance and Trump capped a day that included appearances by some of the other major figures in the GOP, and the party pulled out all the stops to boost morale in the stretch run to the midterms.

Here are the top takeaways from night two of the midterm convention.

Trump's pledge

Facing an energized Democratic Party heading into the midterms, the main mission of the Republican convention was to motivate the GOP's MAGA base, which has a history of sitting it out when Trump isn't on the ballot, to vote this autumn.

Trump reiterated on Thursday evening that his supporters needed to "do me the biggest favor you've ever done...You've got to do this for me. You've got to pretend I'm on the ticket."

The president then led the crowd in a pledge.

FOX NEWS UPDATES FROM THE MIDTERM CONVENTION

"I pledge to the greatest president in the history of America," Trump said as many in the arena repeated his words.

"I am going to go out and I'm going to get my friends, my family, and we are going to vote on November 3rd, or we are going to vote before that," Trump continued before warning that if they didn't cast a ballot, they'd "go to hell."

Trump's unusual pitch

The president repeated his offer to Americans that he announced a night earlier, what he on Thursday described as the "Trump dividend."

On Wednesday, Trump pledged a $5,000 dividend for every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterms.

"We can do that because our country has never done better. We're taking in trillions, trillions of dollars," the president argued.

Trump also showcased his second term achievements, claiming that "in 19 months, I've delivered on every single promise I made."

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

"We delivered the largest tax cuts in American history, the largest regulation cuts in American history, the largest investment in our military in the history of our country, and made America the energy and military superpower of the world," the president proclaimed.

Trump and Republicans are banking that their litany of political wins can rebuff traditional headwinds – the party in power traditionally loses congressional seats in the midterms. The GOP is also battling a rough environment fueled by persistent inflation, a new surge in gas and diesel prices due to a flare-up in the ongoing war with Iran, and a deepening trade war with neighboring Canada.

While Trump touted "tremendous economic success," public opinion polls paint a very different picture, with the president's overall approval rating, and especially his handling of the economy, well into negative territory.

Inflation was a key issue that helped boost Trump and the GOP to sweeping election victories in 2024, but Democrats say affordability has been the issue that fueled their ballot box victories and overperformances since Trump returned to the White House.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC), which remains in debt and decided against holding a similar convention, was more than happy to focus on the economy.

"The only people reaping the benefits of Trump’s economy are himself, his family, and his ultrarich elite donors. Meanwhile, working families get nothing except sky-high receipts at the grocery store and the pump, unaffordable healthcare premiums, and wages that aren’t keeping up with inflation," DNC Rapid Response Director Kendall Witmer charged.

'Radical left lunatics'

Midterm elections are often a referendum on the party in power, but Republicans used their convention to draw a contrast as they spotlighted the Democrats' leftward lurch in this year's primaries and tied the party to far-left and socialist proposals.

"They're not socialists. They're not Democrats, they're communists. We will reject these radical left lunatics," Trump charged for a second straight night.

Vance, in his address minutes earlier, urged Republicans "to send a message this November that the country does not belong to the radicals."

Vance unloads on Democrats

The vice president also argued that Democrats have metastasized into a party that stands against America.

"Let's never forget that America belongs to those who love it, not those who hate it," Vance said.

The vice president also targeted Democrats over combustible issues such as race and immigration. And he took aim at Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in battleground Michigan, for suggesting that Vance's grandfather would object to his marrying a woman of Indian descent.

"This is what he thinks of my grandfather, a man I loved and who loved his family unconditionally. Abdul looks at him, sees the color of his skin, sees his background, and decides that he could never have loved my wife," Vance said.

The vice president argued that Democrats are no longer "the party of FDR or JFK. Hell, they're not even the party of Bill Clinton anymore. The Democrats are the party of hatred. They're the party that despises America and the people who built it."

Ahead of his speech, the DNC claimed that "JD Vance has been Donald Trump’s most loyal puppet."

And the DNC predicted that "Vance will continue to gaslight Americans, but voters know the truth: Trump and Vance have tanked the economy, plunged the country into more endless wars, and failed to make life more affordable for everyday Americans." 

Vance's 2028 moment

While he hasn't said if he'll seek the presidency in 2028, Vance is seen as the front-runner in the race to succeed Trump.

The convention gave Vance the opportunity to appear as a presidential candidate in waiting.

While in Dallas, Vance was warmly received Thursday morning by delegates from key battleground states and he headlined a top-dollar fundraiser for the RNC.

And during his address, the vice president was interrupted by shouts of "48."

But Vance, at least publicly, remains laser focused on 2026.

"We’ve got to take care of business this November, then we’ll worry about what comes next," Vance quickly responded.

item.title: FRANK SILLER: Everyone else was running away on 9/11. My brother ran toward the Twin Towers
item.description: Stephen Siller's brother Frank recounts the FDNY firefighter's final drive toward the World Trade Center through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel on 9/11.
item.content:encoded:
On September 11, 2001, while thousands of people were trying to get away from the danger in lower Manhattan, my brother Stephen was heading straight toward it. His shift as a New York City firefighter was over and he was supposed to meet his brothers for a round of golf, but the moment he heard that a plane had hit the World Trade Center, he turned his truck around. For Stephen, there was never really a choice—people needed help, and he was going to help them.

My brother Stephen barely had time to think when news of a plane hitting the World Trade Center’s North Tower came across the scanner inside his black 1990 GMC Sierra 1500 pickup truck just after 8:46 a.m. on September 11, 2001.

Perhaps that was fitting. In the few seconds that Stephen had to consider whether to keep driving from Brooklyn’s Park Slope neighborhood—where his shift at FDNY Squad 1 had ended just sixteen minutes prior—toward Staten Island, where he was supposed to meet up with the rest of us Siller brothers and head down to central New Jersey and play golf, there was no decision to make. A major accident or attack had just occurred—and countless innocent people needed help. The only direction for Stephen to drive was not away from the fire, but straight toward it.

As golf balls rattled and his clubs whipped to the other side of the truck, Stephen quickly turned around on the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, put his foot on the gas, and began racing in the direction of the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel, where he could drive under the river to lower Manhattan. He could see the thick smoke emanating from lower Manhattan as he tore down the BQE, wondering exactly what had happened and how fast he could get there. Having known Stephen his entire life, I am certain that one question dominated his mind in those frantic yet simultaneously measured few minutes: How many lives can I help save?

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER': THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

At some point while driving as fast as he safely could on the BQE, Stephen called his wife, Sally. He told her that some sort of aircraft had hit the World Trade Center and that even though he’d already finished his overnight shift at the elite Squad 1 in Brooklyn, he was now driving toward lower Manhattan instead of home. Right after he said "I love you" and started getting ready to put down his Nextel phone, Stephen also asked Sally to please let his brothers know that he wouldn’t be able to play golf that day.

Other than saving lives and the well-being of his wife and kids, I believe that there was an additional prominent thought going through Stephen’s mind as he got closer to the tunnel. This is no accident. This is a terrorist attack.

9/11 HERO’S MEMORY PRESERVED THROUGH MASSIVE EFFORT TO ‘DO GOOD’ FOR VETS, FIRST RESPONDERS: ‘HIS LEGACY’

For years, Stephen had told myself and others that it was only a matter of time before New York—and specifically the World Trade Center—would be targeted a second time by international terrorists. He also believed that it was going to be a lot worse than the 1993 bombing, which happened the year before Stephen became a firefighter. While my brother deserves credit for his foresight, his prediction was hardly unique within FDNY ranks, as many senior department leaders (like my friend Sal Cassano) all the way down the totem pole to firefighters like Stephen believed that another attack was imminent. Tragically, they were right.

Stephen’s golf equipment kept bouncing around as he maneuvered among cars like he would ordinarily do while driving his beloved red Chevy. Many of these vehicles had stopped right in the middle of the BQE to watch the terrifying events that were unfolding in the lower Manhattan sky. Stephen, who was urgently trying to reach the mouth of the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel, undoubtedly knew that anything could happen in the next few moments. Yet as Sally could hear in his voice, Stephen was undeterred. Nothing short of an ensuing nuclear missile attack could stop my brother from getting through that tunnel and reaching the Twin Towers.

WHERE TUNNEL TO TOWERS' STEEL ACROSS AMERICA TOUR WILL STOP AHEAD OF 9/11

Robin and Joe Raiso were sitting at that very spot at the mouth of the tunnel after witnessing the surreal sight of the first plane—American Airlines Flight 11—hitting the North Tower. Their car, which had almost made it inside the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel before the NYPD quickly shut it down, was now covered in soot. Even on the Brooklyn side, debris was raining down from a previously bright September sky that was suddenly clouded by smoke and fire.

Naturally, Robin and Joe were both baffled and scared by what they were seeing. They became even more frightened when they heard the screeching sound of a black pickup truck screeching to a stop beside them, on a median. If what was unfolding in the sky above them was some kind of terrorist attack, could the man getting out of his truck be a part of it? Was the tunnel about to be bombed or subjected to another kind of mass casualty incident? A million thoughts raced through Robin’s and Joe’s worried minds.

NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS

That was when they saw my brother. As calmly as possible in the middle of what he correctly assumed was a terrorist attack with sirens blaring, thick black smoke filling the air, and debris falling around him, Stephen got out of his truck, went around back, and started rummaging through the bay of his pickup. After maybe a minute or so, Stephen returned to the front side wearing sixty pounds of firefighter’s gear. Then, without hesitation, my brother started running toward the mouth of the tunnel.

A few moments later, Robin and Joe saw a few NYPD officers stop Stephen in his tracks at the tunnel entrance, which was completely blocked by police barricades. It didn’t take them long to realize that Stephen was indeed an FDNY firefighter, so they nodded, patted Stephen on the back, and let him through.

9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'

"We were shocked and amazed. Everyone was trying to run out," Joe would later say. "He was running in." The last time Robin and Joe saw Stephen was when he ran full speed into the uncertain darkness of the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel. Above him was fire, dust, smoke. In front of my brother was a 1.7-mile path through North America’s longest continuous underwater vehicular tunnel toward the only thing in the world that mattered to him in that moment: the victims of what would soon become known as 9/11. With each step forward, even with that heavy gear on his shoulders and chest, Stephen was closer to helping the helpless.

9/11 DEATH TOLL KEEPS GROWING DECADES LATER AS TOXIC EXPOSURE HAUNTS SURVIVORS

It is difficult, if not impossible, to determine precisely what happened next. Because of Robin and Joe’s eyewitness account, I believe it is most likely that while Stephen was running through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel, the unthinkable—at least for most New Yorkers and Americans who weren’t part of the FDNY, NYPD, or intelligence services—happened in front of millions of eyeballs watching from the ground and on television screens across America. At 9:03 a.m., a second hijacked plane—United Airlines Flight 175—hit the South Tower.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

If Stephen was indeed inside the tunnel when the world as we all knew it changed forever, I can only imagine the tunnel shaking and the deafening sounds that Stephen must have heard. That terrible experience probably made him run even faster—not because he was afraid, but because he knew from the sounds of new explosions that thousands more innocent people were almost certainly in grave danger.

What I cannot imagine is what Stephen saw when he first reached the other side. We know that there was no light at the end of the tunnel—lower Manhattan was covered in darkness and filled with the sounds and smells of fire, smoke, and death.

For Stephen Siller, however, I do believe that he managed to find some light in that darkness. Even amid the chaos, I think my brother knew that his life’s defining moment had arrived.  Going backward was not an option—Stephen’s only direction was forward, toward the innocent people he wanted so desperately to help save.

Stephen’s final run through the Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel has come to represent everything he stood for: courage, sacrifice, and putting others before himself. In his honor, our family started the Tunnel to Towers Foundation to carry that spirit forward and support America’s heroes and their families. To learn more about Stephen’s legacy and our mission, visit T2T.org.

item.title: MIKE PENCE: Remember the fallen — and the generation that defended America since 9/11
item.description: From the World Trade Center to the hunt for Osama bin Laden and ISIS, a generation of Americans answered the call after the September 11 attacks.
item.content:encoded:
On September 11, 2001, shortly after the terrorists struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, I walked across the street to the Capitol, swimming against a sea of pandemonium.

Later, I joined other members in the basement of the Capitol Hill Police headquarters for a briefing on what we knew — and what might happen next.

Former Governor Tom Ridge, then serving as President George W. Bush’s homeland security adviser, told us, "The only thing we know for sure is that they want to hit us again, and they want to hit us worse."

TRUMP CONFIRMS PENTAGON PLANS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 ATTACKS, DISPUTES REPORT ON GROUND ZERO ABSENCE

Long before 2001, radical Islamic terrorism was at war with America’s way of life and had already established a terrible rhythm in our national life.

The 1983 Beirut barracks bombing killed 241 American servicemen. Pan Am Flight 103 was blown out of the sky over Lockerbie, Scotland, in 1988, killing 270 people, including 190 Americans. The first World Trade Center bombing came in 1993: six dead, more than 1,000 injured, with the terrorists hoping to topple one tower into the other. In 1998, al-Qaeda bombed our embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, killing 224 people and injuring thousands. Two years later, al-Qaeda struck again, bombing the USS Cole in Yemen and killing 17 American sailors.

LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11

Our government’s response had fallen into a near slumber of its own. Terrorists attacked. Americans mourned. Investigators pursued those responsible. Security was tightened and warnings were issued. Then life moved on — until the terrorists struck again. For all the courage and skill of those fighting terrorism in those years, America remained largely reactive, responding to attacks rather than preventing them and ensuring that they could never happen again.

September 11 broke that rhythm forever. From the firefighters and police who rushed into the Twin Towers without regard to their personal safety, to those who charged the cockpit in the skies over Pennsylvania, America’s defenders surged forward with what felt like all new resolve to take the fight directly to our terrorist enemies.

HOW 9/11 TRANSFORMED SYNAGOGUE SECURITY INTO A NEW REALITY FOR THE JEWISH COMMUNITY

America resolved that we would no longer simply bring terrorists to justice after they attacked us. We would find them before they could strike, take the fight to them abroad, and build new defenses here at home.

Twenty-five years later, we should remember the heroes forged that day and we should acknowledge the generation of selfless Americans who have delivered on that promise every day since.

In the aftermath of the attacks, young men and women lined up around the block outside military recruiting offices determined to serve our country. Nearly three million American servicemen and women deployed in the wars that followed September 11. More than 7,000 gave their lives and tens of thousands were wounded. They destroyed terrorist sanctuaries, hunted down al-Qaeda leaders, and brought Osama bin Laden to justice.

When ISIS later established a terrorist caliphate across vast stretches of Iraq and Syria, American forces and our allies destroyed it, liberating nearly 110,000 square kilometers of territory and freeing 7.7 million people from its brutal rule.

But, America’s defenders are not found only on distant battlefields. Some chose careers in law enforcement, disrupting terrorist plans on the homefront and chasing leads that never made the evening news. Others joined the Border Patrol, standing watch on the ground while air marshals guarded the skies. In New York City, 58 children of FDNY firefighters who made the ultimate sacrifice on September 11 have grown up to join the same department their fathers served.

Their greatest accomplishment is measured by what did not happen. The nightmare we feared that day — a succession of increasingly catastrophic terrorist attacks on the American homeland — never came to pass.

NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS

Not because our enemies quit trying, but because America’s defenders stopped them cold.

For a generation, Americans have been able to live their lives without the constant fear that another September 11 was around the corner.

That peace was earned by Americans whose names we know and countless others whose names we never will — by those who served both at home and overseas, those who came home wounded, those who never came home at all, and those who still stand watch today.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

On this solemn anniversary, let us remember the 2,977 innocent souls who perished at the hands of our terrorist enemies on September 11.

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

And let us honor those who gave their lives in the long struggle that followed.

Because of the heroes forged that fateful day and every day since, the American people live in freedom and security. So let us offer the thanks of a grateful nation to all who answered the call to protect and defend America these past 25 years.

Our founders proclaimed eternal vigilance is the price of liberty. May we never forget or fail to honor the sacrifices made by America’s defenders from that day to this. And may we never cease to be vigilant in the defense of the land we love. So help us, God.

item.title: Trump admin's list of US-designated 'foreign terrorist' groups in Latin America expands to 21
item.description: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the foreign terrorist designation of Los Tiguerones during his diplomatic tour through Latin America.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration designated an Ecuadorian gang as a "foreign terrorist organization" on Wednesday, extending its list of designated foreign terrorist groups in Latin America and the Caribbean to 21.

The State Department designated Los Tiguerones as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist.

According to the department, Los Tiguerones is an Ecuador-based gang linked to narcotrafficking and other illicit activity, along with several attacks targeting civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists, including the live takeover of an Ecuadorian TV station in 2024.

"The Trump administration will continue to use all available tools to protect our nation by keeping illicit drugs off our streets and disrupting the revenue streams funding violent narcoterrorists," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.

US FORCES SINK NARCO-REFUELING STATION LINKED TO ECUADORIAN CARTEL IN PACIFIC: SOUTHCOM

"Today’s action taken by the State Department further demonstrates that the Trump administration continues to deliver on its promises to the American people to dismantle cartels and narcoterrorist networks in our region, ensuring the safety of the American people," he added.

The announcement came during Rubio's diplomatic tour to South America, where he made stops in Colombia, Ecuador and Peru to address U.S. efforts to combat drug trafficking in Latin America.

The label was previously reserved for terrorist groups such as ISIS and al-Qaida that use violence for political ambitions and not for financially motivated crime organizations like the ones in Latin America and the Caribbean that have recently been added to the list.

But the administration wants to increase pressure on the crime rings and anyone believed to be assisting them.

The government began using the strategy in February 2025, and it served as a pretext for the U.S. capture of then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro earlier this year, as well as dozens of deadly attacks on boats allegedly involved in narcotics trafficking.

The strategy also prompted Latin American countries, including Guatemala and Argentina, to take similar action against certain groups and led Ecuador to launch joint operations on its own soil.

Rubio said terrorist designations "expose and isolate entities and individuals, denying them access to the U.S. financial system and the resources they need to carry out attacks." He also said designations can assist law enforcement actions of other U.S. agencies and governments.

RUBIO DESIGNATES AFGHANISTAN AS 'STATE SPONSOR OF WRONGFUL DETENTION': 'DESPICABLE TACTICS'

Mexico has the most groups of any country on the U.S. list for designated foreign terrorist organizations with eight. The Mexican government is under intense pressure from the U.S. to prevent President Donald Trump from taking unilateral action against cartels in Mexico.

Trump’s approach has also featured contradictions, as he pardoned former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández, who was sentenced to 45 years in prison for drug trafficking and accused during his trial of protecting the Sinaloa Cartel. Hernández has since returned to his country.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Rams' disaster in Australia raises the question: Should the team have followed the 49ers there earlier?
item.description: Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams looked gassed in a 27-7 loss to the San Francisco 49ers in Melbourne as their travel strategy faces scrutiny.
item.content:encoded:
Superteam. Unbeatable. Super Bowl bound.

These were all used to describe the Los Angeles Rams all offseason, yet Week 1 proved why there’s no such thing as a sure thing in the NFL.

The Rams faced their NFC West foe, the San Francisco 49ers, in the NFL’s first-ever game in Australia on Thursday night (or should we say, 10:35 a.m. local time at the Melbourne Cricket Ground) and were dominated in a 27-7 loss to begin the 2026 season.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Let’s be clear: This is no slight to the 49ers, a team many believe will earn a playoff berth in a loaded division. Rather, the noise and astronomical expectations for the Rams made this Week 1 performance a shocker to say the least.

While the "overrated" talk has already begun for football fans on social media, the question must be asked: were the Rams right to fly to Melbourne less than two days before kickoff?

The Rams arrived in Melbourne on Thursday morning local time, with 28 hours until kickoff to begin their season. On the other hand, the 49ers spent close to a week getting adjusted to Melbourne time, practicing multiple times and making sure the team was ready to play a Friday morning game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The approaches were polar opposite, with the Rams arguing they still felt like they were on Los Angeles time, meaning kickoff to them felt like 5:35 p.m. PT on Thursday night.

"What gives me confidence is I’m not going to really make it a big deal," Rams coach Sean McVay said, via The Athletic, regarding the team’s plan to fly so close to gameday. "It’s, ‘Hey, this is what the reality is. We’ve got a long way to go, but let’s be ready to rock when that three-hour window that we’re allotted comes.’"

Both teams did their due diligence in terms of researching the best method and came to two completely different answers. The 49ers consulted sleep experts, coaches and anyone else they could find to see what would be best for the roster.

San Francisco knew the sleep conversation was coming. Considering this was only the NFL’s first game in Australia and the league continues expanding its global reach, it won’t be the last time franchises find themselves Down Under during the regular season.

"People are probably going to speculate after the game, ‘Well, this was better than the other,’" 49ers offensive coordinator Klay Kubiak explained, via the outlet. "But, at the end of the day, we’re going to go out there to play.

"It’s an unprecedented situation. We believe in the way we’re doing it. They believe in the way they’re doing it, and we’re going to play the game."

It seemed pretty clear during these four quarters which team had the better way of doing things with this Australia game.

The 49ers came out buzzing and held that same intensity on both sides of the ball throughout the contest. Meanwhile, the Rams couldn’t find their usual rhythm, especially the reigning MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford.

LOS ANGELES RAMS BETTING OUTLOOK: WHY ONE ANALYST IS ALL IN ON A SUPER BOWL WIN AT +550

Year 18 didn’t begin the way he wanted, seeing just a handful of completions in the first half, though L.A. was only down by three points heading back to the locker room. The Rams scored the first touchdown of the contest early in the second quarter, but Stafford, for the most part, was not his accurate self in key moments.

One of them came after the Rams secured an interception on 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy following the L.A. touchdown drive, which running back Kyren Williams celebrated after busting into the end zone. Stafford was picked off by Renardo Green on a pass intended for Puka Nacua.

And then there was a clear show of force between these two teams when Nacua failed to break the plane on third-and-goal, leaving a fourth-and-goal situation for the Rams and half-a-yard to go. The 49ers just scored a touchdown to open the second half and secure a 17-7 lead.

Stafford went for the quarterback sneak, but he was stuffed right before the goal line, and the 49ers’ defense, which was stellar throughout the game, went ballistic.

To make matters worse, the Rams’ defense, which started the game hot and seemed to lose juice as it went along, gave up a 99-yard touchdown drive to the 49ers after Stafford’s failure to break the plane.

From there, the white flag was virtually raised by McVay on the sideline, sending out Stafford’s backup, Stetson Bennett, and other second-stringers to finish out the lopsided loss.

Also worth noting: Myles Garrett, whom the Rams acquired in a blockbuster trade with the Cleveland Browns this offseason and has an insane impact on the "superteam" debate, didn’t finish with a single stat in his debut. He did deal with a knee situation during training camp, but he looked gassed as he came in and out of the game when the Rams were on defense.

Perhaps his teammates were just as gassed, but it was clear on the scoreboard, and it will likely show up on tape, that the Rams just didn’t have the same energy as their division rival.

Of course, there’s still a long season ahead. Aaron Donald did not travel to Australia with the Rams for his highly anticipated return from retirement, and this squad could still become the juggernaut everyone expects it to be.

But they began the season on the wrong foot and will have a 15-hour flight home to consider whether flying down so late was the right decision.

item.title: ‘I’m coming home’: Last words haunt a 9/11 daughter 25 years later as she builds a legacy in his honor
item.description: Kayla Fallon Smith lost her father in the 9/11 World Trade Center attacks at age 8 and now runs a nonprofit offering equine therapy to veterans.
item.content:encoded:
"I'm getting out. I'm coming home."

Those were the final words of William Lawrence Fallon Jr. before he was killed in the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center 25 years ago.

He worked as an IT manager for Cantor Fitzgerald and was just 38 years old when he was killed.

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

His daughter Kayla Fallon Smith was 8 years old when she learned her father would not be coming home.

Before the attacks, Smith, now 33, said her father – who always commuted into work early – would call the house phone in the morning to wish her and her sister well before they would head to school.

📸 Instagram: kelsiecairns_tv

🎥 Facebook: Kelsie Cairns

He went in early so he could leave earlier in the afternoons to take her to dancing school after her school day.

"That was the kind of man he was. I remember he would get up and work out in the morning before even going to work, so you'd hear the weights dropping in the house. I do remember that as a kid," Smith said.

Those quick and light-hearted morning phone calls to his daughters set the tone for the day.

"He would tell us what the skyline looked like. Sometimes it would be cloudy below him and he couldn't even see the street, but it'd be sunny up there," she said.

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

Smith remembers hearing her father's voice for the last time on Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001.

"I spoke to him on the house phone that day, as I always did," she said, to which he said on the phone, "Have a good morning," she said.

"I'm sure I said something like, 'I love you, have a great day'," Smith said.

Her dad called again that fateful morning – sometime after the first tower was hit.

SALVATION ARMY RESPONDER OPENS UP ON 9/11 CANCER BATTLE, PHONE CALL THAT CHANGED HIS LIFE

This time, her mother answered the phone.

"He said something to the degree of, 'I'm getting out, I'm coming home,' and that was it," she said.

Smith's mother replied and said, "What are you talking about?" He responded and said, "Turn on the news."

After that he hung up.

9/11 DEATH TOLL KEEPS GROWING DECADES LATER AS TOXIC EXPOSURE HAUNTS SURVIVORS

His family never heard from him again.

"Those words haunt me a little bit," Smith said. "Every year, grief is different. It doesn't go away. It's a myth when people say that time heals all wounds; it doesn't."

In the last 25 years of growing up without her father, Smith has turned her pain and grief into purpose. She's devoted her life to helping others living with grief and mental struggles.

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Smith is a licensed mental health counselor who founded Trails of Purpose – a nonprofit organization that provides free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members, veterans, first responders and their families.

"As I was getting my graduate degree, I started to experience equine-assisted therapy, and I really—it just clicked for me," she said.

She went on to say, "I never experienced that as a kid, and I had a lot of trauma therapy growing up. The resources were abundant for 9/11 victims, and I never experienced equine therapy."

She started her organization in 2019.

"I needed a place to just be when my brain always felt on fire. I think I've created that, and it's seeming to resonate with other people."

SEND US A TIP

Trails of Purpose has offered 30,000 hours of free mental health counseling and equine-assisted therapy to military members and first responders.

"The horses, and the connection that they have when when words don't seem to to come, the horses can just be with you," she said.

"I created the thing that I think I needed: community and understanding, and a place that's safe, and quiet, and a respite," she said.

As she helps others heal, Smith said she'll never stop sharing her father's story.

"If we can remember the feeling that we had on September 12th, I think that would be my biggest point of education for the next generation."

item.title: American Jessica Pegula falls to top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka in straight sets in US Open semifinal
item.description: Aryna Sabalenka dominated Jessica Pegula with 29 winners to reach the U.S. Open final, where Coco Gauff or Elena Rybakina awaits Saturday night.
item.content:encoded:
The current World No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka moved one step closer to a third consecutive U.S. Open title Thursday, defeating third-ranked Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 in the women’s singles semifinal in New York.

The match was even through most of the first set, but Sabalenka found another gear late, taking advantage of Pegula’s second serve and carrying that momentum into the second set. She turned the final set into arguably her most impressive stretch of tennis in the tournament.

"No complaints," the 28-year-old Belarusian tennis star said after securing a spot in Saturday's final. "I’m just super happy that I was able to pull out such tennis."

ARYNA SABALENKA FIRES BACK AT REPORTER FOR ASKING QUESTION ABOUT PARTYING AFTER US OPEN VICTORY

Sabalenka will face the winner of the semifinal between No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina and No. 4 seed Coco Gauff on Saturday. A win over either opponent would make her the first women’s player since Serena Williams from 2012-14 to win three consecutive U.S. Open titles.

Rybakina will replace Sabalenka atop the women’s tennis rankings next week, and Sabalenka said this week she would be fine ceding No. 1 after she held it.

It will be hard to prevent that if she hits the ball Saturday the way she did against Pegula.

Sabalenka pounded 29 winners to Pegula’s 12, turning their third straight meeting at the end of the U.S. Open into a rout, after her victory in the 2024 final and 2025 semifinals were tight most of the way.

"I was so desperate for the win, I wanted it badly," Sabalenka said.
